title: Real numbers
competency: Define real numbers, compare them, and find real numbers between any two real numbers.

keywords.def: Any rational or irrational number. Every point on the number line is a real number. The set is written ℝ.
A number that can be written a/b with integers a, b and b ≠ 0. The set is written ℚ.
A decimal that neither ends nor repeats, such as √2 or π. It cannot be written as a/b.
For real a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b, a > b is true.
If a < b and b < c, then a < c.

en.text: A real number is either rational or irrational. Together they make the set ℝ. Every decimal is exactly one point on the number line. Every point on the line is exactly one decimal.

screens.title: Two lists, one set?
screens.text: Abebe lists 3/4, −2 and 0.5. Almaz lists √2 and π. Activity 1.14 asks about such lists.
screens.ask: Is there one set that holds both lists?
opts: Yes, one set holds them all
Only Abebe's list is a set
screens.after:
Yes. Every number in both lists is a real number.
The set of real numbers ℝ holds rationals and irrationals together.
Read on for the book's definition.
screens.best: Yes, one set holds them all

screens.title: Real numbers
paras: Activity 1.14 asks: how are points on the number line and decimals related?
Every decimal, rational or irrational, is exactly one point on the number line. Every point is exactly one decimal.
Definition 1.7: A number is a real number if it is either rational or irrational.
The set of real numbers, ℝ, is the union of the rational and the irrational numbers: ℝ = {x : x is rational or x is irrational}.
screens.note: The real numbers are made of two non-overlapping parts: rational and irrational.

screens.title: Real numbers
defs: A number that is either rational or irrational. The set of all real numbers is written ℝ.

screens.title: Which is true?
screens.text: Real numbers: which statement is true?
opts: Some numbers are both rational and irrational
π is not a real number
screens.why:
ℝ is made of two parts: the rationals and the irrationals.
So every irrational number is in ℝ: it is real.
"Every real number is rational" is false: √2 is real but not rational.
No number is both, and π is real.
screens.clue: The two parts of ℝ do not overlap, and together they fill it.

screens.title: Rational or irrational?
screens.text: Every one of these is a real number. Sort them into the two parts of ℝ.
items: It is a fraction of two integers.
Its decimal neither ends nor repeats.
screens.why:
A rational decimal ends or repeats: 3/4 = 0.75, −7 = −7/1, 0.333… = 1/3.
An irrational decimal never ends and never repeats: √2 = 1.41421…, π = 3.14159…
Both groups are real numbers.
screens.clue: Ask: does the decimal end or repeat?

screens.title: Fill in the set
screens.ask: Complete the definition: ℝ is the union of the rational numbers and the ___ numbers.
screens.why:
Definition 1.7: a real number is rational or irrational.
So ℝ = rationals ∪ irrationals.
The missing word is "irrational".
screens.clue: Which kind of number is not rational?

screens.title: A plot in Bahir Dar
screens.text: True or false? Hana has a square plot in Bahir Dar with area 2 m². Its side is √2 m. The side length is a real number.
screens.why:
Side × side = 2, so the side is √2 m.
√2 = 1.41421… never ends or repeats: it is irrational.
Every irrational number is real.
So the statement is true.
screens.clue: Is √2 rational or irrational? Both kinds belong to ℝ.
screens.worked: √2 = 1.41421… never ends or repeats, so it is irrational. Irrational numbers are real. So the side is a real number.

en.text: Each real number is one point on the number line, so any two can be compared. Exactly one of a < b, a = b, a > b is true. For non-negative numbers, compare the squares. Between any two real numbers there are infinitely many more.

screens.title: Which is bigger?
screens.text: Look at √3/6 and 2/3. One has a root, one does not.
screens.ask: Which number is bigger? Take a guess.
screens.after:
2/3 ≈ 0.667 and √3/6 ≈ 1.732 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.289.
So 2/3 is bigger.
The book shows a way without a calculator: square both. Read on.

screens.title: Comparing real numbers
paras: Each real number is one point on the number line. So any two real numbers can be compared.
Trichotomy: for real a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b, a > b is true.
Transitive: if a < b and b < c, then a < c.
For non-negative a and b: if a² < b², then a < b.

screens.title: Compare on the number line
screens.ask: Tap each point. The one further right is bigger.

points.info: ≈ 0.289. It is the smallest here: furthest left.

screens.title: Two rules of order
defs: For real a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b, a > b is true.
If a < b and b < c, then a < c.

screens.title: Use the transitive rule
screens.text: Transitive property: you know that a < b and b < c.
screens.why:
a < b: a is left of b on the number line.
b < c: b is left of c.
So a is left of c: a < c.
This is the transitive property.
screens.clue: Place a, b and c on a number line.

screens.text: Four ways to compare real numbers.
steps: (a) −8 is left of −2 on the number line, so −8 < −2.

screens.title: Compare by squaring
screens.text: Compare by squaring: which is true about 3√2 and 2√3?
screens.why:
Both numbers are positive, so compare their squares.
(3√2)² = 3² × 2 = 9 × 2 = 18.
(2√3)² = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.
18 > 12, so 3√2 > 2√3.
screens.worked: (3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18. (2√3)² = 4 × 3 = 12. Both numbers are positive and 18 > 12, so 3√2 > 2√3.

screens.title: Real numbers between two numbers
paras: Is there a real number between 2 and 4.2? Take the average: (2 + 4.2)/2 = 3.1, and 2 < 3.1 < 4.2.
Averaging again gives 2.55, between 2 and 3.1. It also gives 3.65, between 3.1 and 4.2.
We can keep doing this for ever. So there are infinitely many real numbers between any two real numbers.

screens.title: Halve the gap again and again
screens.ask: Tap the points. Each new one is an average of two others.

points.info: The other end. We can keep averaging for ever.

screens.title: Find one in between
screens.text: Find a number in between: which number is between 1/3 and 1/2?
screens.clue: Take the average of the two numbers.

screens.title: Teff prices in Adama
screens.text: One shop in Adama sells a kilo of teff for 95 birr. Another sells it for 101 birr. A third shop charges the average of the two.
screens.ask: Find the average price: the third shop charges ___ birr.
screens.clue: Add the two prices, then divide by 2.

items.why:
Line up the digits: 0.236 and 0.256.
Tenths: 2 and 2, the same.
Hundredths: 3 < 5.
So 0.236 < 0.256.
items.clue: Compare digit by digit from the left.

items.why:
First compare without signs: 0.1350 < 0.1351.
So −0.135 is closer to 0 than −0.1351.
Closer to 0 means further right, so bigger.
So −0.135 > −0.1351.
items.clue: For negatives, the one closer to 0 is bigger.

items.text: Compare a root with a decimal: √5/2 ☐ 0.234
Compare a fraction with π: 22/7 ☐ π
items.why:
22 ÷ 7 = 3.142857…
π = 3.141592…
Third decimal place: 2 > 1.
So 22/7 > π. 22/7 is only an estimate of π.
items.clue: Write both as decimals to 4 places.

items.why:
Both numbers are positive, so compare squares.
(6√5)² = 36 × 5 = 180.
(5√7)² = 25 × 7 = 175.
180 > 175, so 6√5 > 5√7.

items.text: Compare a sum with a root: 2 + √3 ☐ 4
Find a number in between: which real number is between −0.24 and −0.246?
items.why:
Write −0.24 as −0.240.
We need a number from −0.246 up to −0.240.
−0.246 < −0.245 < −0.240, so −0.245 works.
−0.25 and −0.247 are too far left; −0.2 is too far right.

items.text: Find a number in between: which real number is between 3/5 and 2/7?
items.why:
2/7 = 0.2857… and 3/5 = 0.6.
We need a number between 0.286 and 0.6.
0.4 fits: 0.286 < 0.4 < 0.6.
0.2 and 0.25 are too small; 0.7 is too big.

items.text: Find a number in between: which real number is between √2 and √3?
items.clue: Check by squaring: is the square between 2 and 3?

items.text: Density of ℝ: how many real numbers are there between two different real numbers?
items.why:
The average of two numbers lies between them.
Average again with either end: another number between.
This never stops.
So there are infinitely many.
items.clue: Think about averaging again and again.

test.text: True or false? Some real numbers are neither rational nor irrational.
test.why:
Definition 1.7: a real number is rational or irrational.
There is no third kind.
So the statement is false.

test.text: Compare by squaring: which is true about √3/6 and 2/3?
test.why:
Both are positive, so compare their squares.
(√3/6)² = 3/36.
(2/3)² = 4/9 = 16/36.
3/36 < 16/36, so √3/6 < 2/3.

test.ask: Find a number in between: the average of 2 and 4.2 is ___.

screens.title: Rational or irrational?
screens.text: Look at the decimal form of the number.
steps: A rational number can be written a/b, with integers a, b and b ≠ 0.
Its decimal ends, like 0.75, or repeats, like 0.333…
An irrational decimal neither ends nor repeats.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.why:
0.75 ends and 0.333… repeats: both are rational.
22/7 is a fraction of integers: rational.
√2 = 1.41421… never ends and never repeats.
So √2 is irrational.
screens.clue: Which decimal neither ends nor repeats?

screens.title: Your turn
screens.why:
(3√2)² = 3² × (√2)².
3² = 9 and (√2)² = 2.
9 × 2 = 18.
6 is a slip: it doubles instead of squaring.
screens.clue: Square the 3 and square the √2 separately.
